{{Infobox magazine | title = Jewish Sports Review | image_file = | image_size = | image_alt = | image_caption = | editor = Ephraim Moxson; Shel Wallman | editor_title = Editors | previous_editor = | staff_writer = Neil Keller; Stan Ramati | frequency = Bi-monthly | circulation = | category = Jewish Sports | company = | publisher = Ephraim Moxson; Shel Wallman | firstdate = May–June 1997[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/Subscriptions.html] | country = U.S. | based = [[Los Angeles, California]][http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/About-Us.html] | language = | website = [http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/ www.jewishsportsreview.com] | issn = }} The '''''Jewish Sports Review''''' (''JSR'') is a bi-monthly magazine that was established in 1997.[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/][http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/Subscriptions.html][http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html][http://theminaretonline.com/2010/04/28/article11429][http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1141512/index.htm][http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/2000/01/13/2000-01-13_film_recalls_greenberg_war_v.html] Its editors are Ephraim Moxson and Shel Wallman. The magazine identifies which star and professional athletes are Jewish.[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/][http://theminaretonline.com/2010/04/28/article11429][http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1141512/index.htm] It also covers and has all-time lists for Jewish players in major league baseball,[http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/sport/archives/2009/07/03/2003447694][http://www.clevelandjewishnews.com/articles/2010/04/16/arts/jewish_stars/doc4bc77d3bbc236279484076.txt] pro football,[http://www.sanfranciscosentinel.com/?p=71276] pro basketball,[http://www.clevelandjewishnews.com/articles/2010/01/22/arts/jewish_stars/doc4b58c3eeb6312045104359.txt] and pro hockey;[http://www.clevelandjewishnews.com/articles/2010/01/22/arts/jewish_stars/doc4b58c3eeb6312045104359.txt][http://www.jweekly.com/article/full/41080/jews-and-mel-on-the-big-screen-winter-sports-roundup/][http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html] selects Jewish All-America College teams in baseball,[http://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=news&oi=news_result&ct=res&cd=4&ved=0CDcQqQIwAw&url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.courierpostonline.com%2Farticle%2F20100422%2FSPORTS%2F4220346%2F1002%2Fsports&ei=9lDqS4uYDoK0lQeMgYnVCg&usg=AFQjCNEQ36GdmOMaJjNLofkJY8EdQTlDmw&sig2=yfKr6QP7HgaJkNkgKGlnCQ] football, basketball,[http://bearsports.wustl.edu/releases/mbk5-6-10.html] softball,[http://www.northshoreoflongisland.com/Articles-i-2008-07-24-73420.113114_Jacobs_Kavitsky_honored_for_softball_efforts.html] soccer,[http://www.cstv.com/sports/w-soccer/stories/012705aaa.html] and lacrosse;[http://media.www.thetriangle.org/media/storage/paper689/news/2004/08/20/Sports/Jewish.Sports.Review.Honors.Lacrosse.Player-703300.shtml] covers international athletic events;[http://www.clevelandjewishnews.com/articles/2010/02/12/arts/jewish_stars/doc4b74847fd85a4658916074.txt] selects high school Jewish All-America teams in basketball; and names the top graduating Jewish high school athletes.[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/][http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/03/24/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt] In addition, it covers "minor sports", such as boxing.[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/][http://www.nytimes.com/2003/07/26/sports/boxing-one-fight-too-many-costs-boxer-his-life.html?pagewanted=1] As to his inspiration for launching the magazine, Wallman—speaking on a panel on Jews in baseball at the Cooperstown [[Baseball Hall of Fame]]—said: "I was always curious to know who was Jewish as a kid. And there wasn't a list."[http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt] ==Jewish athletes== The ''JSR'' provides information as to who is Jewish in the sports world, verifying the Jewish background of every athlete covered.[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/][http://theminaretonline.com/2010/04/28/article11429][http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1141512/index.htm] Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward."[http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html] ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.[http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt][http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/] If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish).[http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/] Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.[http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463] ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.[http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2]
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students.[http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html] Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks.[http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html] Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]][http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).[http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1141512/index.htm][http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/] ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.[http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk] The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel.[http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/2000/01/13/2000-01-13_film_recalls_greenberg_war_v.html] And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season.[http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/sports/2000/01/13/2000-01-13_film_recalls_greenberg_war_v.html] When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.[http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt][http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/][http://www.boston.com/news/globe/living/articles/2003/10/13/tribute_is_in_the_cards_for_jewish_ballplayers/] Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, teams in it would recruit top college baseball players from the ''JSR'''s Jewish All-Americans in [[NCAA]] Divisions I, II, and III.[http://www.studlife.com/archives/Sports/2007/09/12/FromKellyFieldtotheFieldofDreams/] ==Basketball== [[File:Scheyer.jpg|right|thumb|180px|[[Jon Scheyer]]]] After [[Jon Scheyer]], later an [[2010 NCAA Men's Basketball All-Americans|All-American]] captain of the [[2009–10 Duke Blue Devils men's basketball team|2010 Duke national championship team]], led his high school team of five Jewish starters to an Illinois state championship, ''[[The Forward]]'' quoted Wallman as speculating that an all-Jewish starting lineup may have won a state title in the 1940s, but that it hadn’t happened in the recent past. ==In the media== Peter Horvitz, in ''The Big Book of Jewish Sports Heroes: An Illustrated Compendium of Sports History and The 150 Greatest Jewish Sports Stars'' (2007), calls Wallman the "best and most dependable source of up-to-date information on the subject" of Jews in sports.[http://books.google.com/books?id=voCnkWSOoRsC&pg=PA7&dq=%22jewish+sports+review%22&hl=en&ei=_UXqS8KcNMP58AaVgaXoDg&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=2&ved=0CDkQ6AEwAQ#v=onepage&q=%22jewish%20sports%20review%22&f=false] Joseph Siegman, in his book ''Jewish sports legends: the International Jewish Hall of Fame'' (2005), listed Moxson as a distinguished authority on sports.[http://books.google.com/books?id=oZxnNt28DhcC&pg=PA240&dq=%22jewish+sports+review%22&hl=en&ei=_UXqS8KcNMP58AaVgaXoDg&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=3&ved=0CD4Q6AEwAg#v=onepage&q=%22jewish%20sports%20review%22&f=false] ''[[The New York Times]]'' noted that the ''JSR'' "aims to be rigorously comprehensive".[http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html] ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' called the JSR "tireless in its service mission".[http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1141512/index.htm] The ''JSR'' has been featured in ''Sports Illustrated'',[http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1141512/index.htm] ''The New York Times'',[http://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/25/nyregion/neighborhood-report-upper-west-side-honoring-yes-the-jewish-athlete.html] ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', and ''[[Baltimore Sun]]''.[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/] ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== *[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/ ''Jewish Sports Review'']

And there wasn't a list."{{cite web|last=Ephross |first=Peter |url=http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt |title=:: Welcome To The Jewish Ledger :: |publisher=Jewishledger.com |date=September 22, 2004 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Jewish athletes== The ''JSR'' provides information as to who is Jewish in the sports world, verifying the Jewish background of every athlete covered.{{cite web|url=http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/ |title=Home |publisher=Jewish Sports Review |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk - February 6, 2007 - The New York Sun |publisher=Nysun.com |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. And there wasn't a list."{{cite web|last=Ephross |first=Peter |url=http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt |title=:: Welcome To The Jewish Ledger :: |publisher=Jewishledger.com |date=September 22, 2004 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Jewish athletes== The ''JSR'' provides information as to who is Jewish in the sports world, verifying the Jewish background of every athlete covered. Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk – February 6, 2007 – The New York Sun |publisher=Nysun.com |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite web|last=Lowenfish |first=Lee |url=http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/ |title=New Cards Mine Baseball’s Jewish Bench – The Jewish Daily Forward |publisher=Forward.com |date=March 24, 2006 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Cobb |first=Nathan |url=http://www.boston.com/news/globe/living/articles/2003/10/13/tribute_is_in_the_cards_for_jewish_ballplayers/ |title=/ News / Boston Globe / Living / Arts / Tribute is in the cards for Jewish ballplayers |publisher=Boston.com |date=October 13, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk – February 6, 2007 – The New York Sun |publisher=Nysun.com |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk – February 6, 2007 – The New York Sun |publisher=Nysun.com |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite web|last=Lowenfish |first=Lee |url=http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/ |title=New Cards Mine Baseball’s Jewish Bench – The Jewish Daily Forward |publisher=Forward.com |date=March 24, 2006 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Cobb |first=Nathan |url=http://www.boston.com/news/globe/living/articles/2003/10/13/tribute_is_in_the_cards_for_jewish_ballplayers/ |title=/ News / Boston Globe / Living / Arts / Tribute is in the cards for Jewish ballplayers |publisher=Boston.com |date=October 13, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, teams in it would recruit top college baseball players from the ''JSR'''s Jewish All-Americans in [[NCAA]] Divisions I, II, and III.{{cite web|last=Wieczorek |first=Allie |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} In addition, it covers "minor sports", such as boxing.{{cite news|last=Gray |first=Geoffrey |url=http://www.nytimes.com/2003/07/26/sports/boxing-one-fight-too-many-costs-boxer-his-life.html?pagewanted=1 |title=BOXING – BOXING – One Fight Too Many Costs Boxer His Life |publisher=NYTimes.com |date=July 26, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} As to his inspiration for launching the magazine, Wallman—speaking on a panel on Jews in baseball at the Cooperstown [[Baseball Hall of Fame]]—said: "I was always curious to know who was Jewish as a kid. And there wasn't a list."{{cite web|last=Ephross |first=Peter |url=http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt |title=:: Welcome To The Jewish Ledger :: |publisher=Jewishledger.com |date=September 22, 2004 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Jewish athletes== The ''JSR'' provides information as to who is Jewish in the sports world, verifying the Jewish background of every athlete covered. Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk – February 6, 2007 – The New York Sun |publisher=Nysun.com |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite web|last=Lowenfish |first=Lee |url=http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/ |title=New Cards Mine Baseball’s Jewish Bench – The Jewish Daily Forward |publisher=Forward.com |date=March 24, 2006 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Cobb |first=Nathan |url=http://www.boston.com/news/globe/living/articles/2003/10/13/tribute_is_in_the_cards_for_jewish_ballplayers/ |title=/ News / Boston Globe / Living / Arts / Tribute is in the cards for Jewish ballplayers |publisher=Boston.com |date=October 13, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, teams in it would recruit top college baseball players from the ''JSR'''s Jewish All-Americans in [[NCAA]] Divisions I, II, and III.{{cite web|last=Wieczorek |first=Allie |url=http://www.studlife.com/archives/Sports/2007/09/12/FromKellyFieldtotheFieldofDreams/ |title=From Kelly Field to the ‘Field of Dreams’ |publisher=Studlife.com |date=September 12, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Basketball== [[File:Scheyer.jpg|right|thumb|180px|[[Jon Scheyer]]]] After [[Jon Scheyer]], later an [[2010 NCAA Men's Basketball All-Americans|All-American]] captain of the [[2009–10 Duke Blue Devils men's basketball team|2010 Duke national championship team]], led his high school team of five Jewish starters to an Illinois state championship, ''[[The Forward]]'' quoted Wallman as speculating that an all-Jewish starting lineup may have won a state title in the 1940s, but that it hadn’t happened in the recent past. ==In the media== Peter Horvitz, in ''The Big Book of Jewish Sports Heroes: An Illustrated Compendium of Sports History and The 150 Greatest Jewish Sports Stars'' (2007), calls Wallman the "best and most dependable source of up-to-date information on the subject" of Jews in sports.{{cite web|url=http://books.google.com/books?id=voCnkWSOoRsC&pg=PA7&dq=%22jewish+sports+review%22&hl=en&ei=_UXqS8KcNMP58AaVgaXoDg&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=2&ved=0CDkQ6AEwAQ#v=onepage&q=%22jewish%20sports%20review%22&f=false |title=The Big Book of Jewish Sports Heros ... – Google Books |publisher=Books.google.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Joseph Siegman, in his book ''Jewish sports legends: the International Jewish Hall of Fame'' (2005), listed Moxson as a distinguished authority on sports.{{cite web|url=http://books.google.com/books?id=oZxnNt28DhcC&pg=PA240&dq=%22jewish+sports+review%22&hl=en&ei=_UXqS8KcNMP58AaVgaXoDg&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=3&ved=0CD4Q6AEwAg#v=onepage&q=%22jewish%20sports%20review%22&f=false |title=Jewish sports legends: the ... – Google Books |publisher=Books.google.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ''[[The New York Times]]'' noted that the ''JSR'' "aims to be rigorously The ''JSR'' has been featured in ''Sports Illustrated'', ''The New York Times'', ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', and ''[[Baltimore Sun]]''. ==See also== *[[List of Jews in sports]] www.NeilKeller.com ==References== {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== *[http://www.jewishsportsreview.com/ ''Jewish Sports Review''] {{Organized Jewish Life in the United States}} [[Category:Sports magazines]] [[Category:Jewish magazines published in the United States]] [[Category:Magazines published in California]] [[Category:Biweekly magazines]] [[Category:Magazines established in 1997]]

And there wasn't a list."{{cite web|last=Ephross |first=Peter |url=http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt |title=:: Welcome To The Jewish Ledger :: |publisher=Jewishledger.com |date=September 22, 2004 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Jewish athletes== The ''JSR'' provides information as to who is Jewish in the sports world, verifying the Jewish background of every athlete covered. Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=Njjewishnews.com |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | Charlotte | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte.creativeloafing.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk – February 6, 2007 – The New York Sun |publisher=Nysun.com |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite web|last=Lowenfish |first=Lee |url=http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/ |title=New Cards Mine Baseball’s Jewish Bench – The Jewish Daily Forward |publisher=Forward.com |date=March 24, 2006 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Cobb |first=Nathan |url=http://www.boston.com/news/globe/living/articles/2003/10/13/tribute_is_in_the_cards_for_jewish_ballplayers/ |title=/ News / Boston Globe / Living / Arts / Tribute is in the cards for Jewish ballplayers |publisher=Boston.com |date=October 13, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, teams in it would recruit top college baseball players from the ''JSR'''s Jewish All-Americans in [[NCAA]] Divisions I, II, and III.{{cite web|last=Wieczorek |first=Allie Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. Cooperstown [[Baseball Hall of Fame]]—said: "I was always curious to know who was Jewish as a kid. And there wasn't a list."{{cite web|last=Ephross |first=Peter |url=http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt |title=:: |publisher=Jewishledger.com |date=September 22, 2004 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Jewish athletes== The ''JSR'' provides information as to who is Jewish in the sports world, verifying the Jewish background of every athlete covered. Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=The [[New Jersey Jewish News]] |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Rodman |first=Edmon J. |url=http://www.jta.org/news/article/2010/10/28/2741474/jewish-review-headline |title=Duo celebrating bar mitzvah of counting Jewish athletes |publisher=JTA |date= |accessdate=October 29, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte [[Creative Loafing]] |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the JSR researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk |publisher=The New York Sun |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite web|last=Lowenfish |first=Lee |url=http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/ |title=New Cards Mine Baseball’s Jewish Bench|publisher=Forward |date=March 24, 2006 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite |publisher=Boston.com |date=October 13, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, teams in it would recruit top college baseball players from the ''JSR'''s Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=The [[New Jersey Jewish News]] |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Rodman |first=Edmon J. |url=http://www.jta.org/news/article/2010/10/28/2741474/jewish-review-headline |title=Duo celebrating bar mitzvah of counting Jewish athletes |publisher=JTA |date= |accessdate=October 29, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he doesn't identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte [[Creative Loafing]] |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the ''JSR'' researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk |publisher=The New York Sun |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|222px|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite web|last=Lowenfish |first=Lee |url=http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/ |title=New Cards Mine Baseball’s Jewish Bench|publisher=Forward |date=March 24, 2006 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Cobb |first=Nathan |url=http://www.boston.com/news/globe/living/articles/2003/10/13/tribute_is_in_the_cards_for_jewish_ballplayers/ |title= Tribute is in the cards for Jewish ballplayers |publisher=Boston.com |date=October 13, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, teams in it would recruit top college baseball players from the ''JSR'''s Jewish All-Americans in [[NCAA]] Divisions I, II, and III.{{cite web|last=Wieczorek |first=Allie |url=http://www.studlife.com/archives/Sports/2007/09/12/FromKellyFieldtotheFieldofDreams/ |title=From Kelly Field to the ‘Field of Dreams’ |publisher=Studlife.com |date=September 12, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Basketball== [[File:Scheyer.jpg|right|thumb|180px|[[Jon Scheyer]]]] After [[Jon Scheyer]], later an [[2010 NCAA Men's Basketball All-Americans|All-American]] captain of the [[2009–10 Duke Blue Devils men's basketball team|2010 Duke national championship team]], led his high school team of five Jewish starters to an Illinois state championship, ''[[The Forward]]'' quoted Wallman as speculating that an all-Jewish starting lineup may have won a state title in the 1940s, but that it hadn’t happened in the recent past. ==In the media== Peter Horvitz, in ''The Big Book of Jewish Sports Heroes: An Illustrated Compendium of Sports History and The 150 Greatest Jewish Sports Stars'' (2007), calls Wallman the "best and most dependable source of up-to-date information on the subject" of Jews in sports.{{cite book|url=http://books.google.com/books?id=voCnkWSOoRsC&pg=PA7&dq=%22jewish+sports+review%22&hl=en&ei=_UXqS8KcNMP58AaVgaXoDg&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=2&ved=0CDkQ6AEwAQ#v=onepage&q=%22jewish%20sports%20review%22&f=false|author=Peter Horvitz |title=The Big Book of Jewish Sports Heros: An Illustrated Compendium of Sports History and The 150 Greatest JEwish Sports Stars|publisher=Books.google.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Joseph Siegman, in his book ''Jewish sports legends: the International Jewish Hall of Fame'' (2005), listed Moxson as a distinguished authority on sports.{{cite book|url=http://books.google.com/books?id=oZxnNt28DhcC&pg=PA240&dq=%22jewish+sports+review%22&hl=en&ei=_UXqS8KcNMP58AaVgaXoDg&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=3&ved=0CD4Q6AEwAg#v=onepage&q=%22jewish%20sports%20review%22&f=false|author=Joseph rigorously comprehensive". ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' called the JSR "tireless in its service mission". Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=The [[New Jersey Jewish News]] |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Rodman |first=Edmon J. |url=http://www.jta.org/news/article/2010/10/28/2741474/jewish-review-headline |title=Duo celebrating bar mitzvah of counting Jewish athletes |publisher=JTA |date= |accessdate=October 29, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he does not identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte [[Creative Loafing]] |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the ''JSR'' researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}

|url=http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/03/24/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt |title=:: |publisher=Jewish Ledger |date=March 24, 2004 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} In addition, it covers "minor sports", such as boxing.{{cite news|last=Gray |first=Geoffrey |url=http://www.nytimes.com/2003/07/26/sports/boxing-one-fight-too-many-costs-boxer-his-life.html?pagewanted=1 |title=One Fight Too Many Costs Boxer His Life |publisher=NYTimes.com |date=July 26, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} As to his inspiration for launching the magazine, Wallman—speaking on a panel on Jews in baseball at the Cooperstown [[Baseball Hall of Fame]]—said: "I was always curious to know who was Jewish as a kid. And there wasn't a list."{{cite web|last=Ephross |first=Peter |url=http://www.jewishledger.com/articles/2004/09/22/news/on_the_cover/news02.txt |title=:: |publisher=Jewishledger.com |date=September 22, 2004 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Jewish athletes== The ''JSR'' provides information as to who is Jewish in the sports world, verifying the Jewish background of every athlete covered. Wallman said: "These days, most Jewish parents with a kid who has a good chance to play in the pros will encourage them," adding with a smile, "You can always go to medical school afterward." ===Criteria=== The ''JSR'''s criteria are that an athlete is Jewish if one of his parents is Jewish, he did not practice any other religion while he played, and he identified ethnically as a member of the Jewish community.{{cite web|url=http://njjewishnews.com/kaplanskorner/2008/11/05/the-phone-books-here-the-phone-books-here/ |title=“The phone book’s here, the phone book’s here!” * » Kaplan’s Korner on Jews and Sports |publisher=The [[New Jersey Jewish News]] |date=January 4, 2010 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite web|last=Rodman |first=Edmon J. |url=http://www.jta.org/news/article/2010/10/28/2741474/jewish-review-headline |title=Duo celebrating bar mitzvah of counting Jewish athletes |publisher=JTA |date= |accessdate=October 29, 2010}} If an athlete has a Jewish parent but was raised in, or converted to, another faith, or indicated to the ''JSR'' that he did not wish to be considered Jewish, he is excluded (even though under Jewish law he might be considered Jewish). Moxson indicates that [[David Beckham]] is not included, as only his mother's father is Jewish, and he does not identify himself as Jewish.{{cite web|last=Salkin |first=Allen |url=http://charlotte.creativeloafing.com/gyrobase/where_have_you_gone_sandy_koufax_/Content?oid=4463 |title=Where have you gone, Sandy Koufax? | News | Cover |publisher=Charlotte [[Creative Loafing]] |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ===Verification=== Columnist Nate Bloom described how the ''JSR'' researches whether an athlete is Jewish as follows:
Every once in a while, the Review adds a player because he is clearly identified as Jewish in a very good news source like an interview. More often, they decide to contact a player (or a player's representative, or very close family member)--because of a tip or because the player has a "Jewish sounding" name. If they are told (by the player or his rep) that the player has one or more Jewish parents—they then inquire if the player was raised in and/or currently adheres to a faith other than Judaism. If the player answers "yes" to either of those questions—that ends the Review's inquiries and they don't cover the player. On the other hand, if they are told the player was raised Jewish or "nothing"--the Review then asks if the player has any objection to being identified as Jewish in the pages of the Review. If not, then they add him.{{cite web|last=Bloom |first=Nate |url=http://www.interfaithfamily.com/arts_and_entertainment/popular_culture/Interfaith_Celebrities_Play_Ball.shtml?rd=2 |title=Interfaith Celebrities Play Ball |publisher=InterfaithFamily.com |date= |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}
The magazine get tips on athletes from their subscribers, public relations directors for pro teams, school coaches, parents, and students. Wallman searches by phone and on the internet for top Jewish athletes in pro, college, and high school ranks. Some athletes are not "obviously" Jewish, such as former major league baseball player, [[Ruben Amaro, Jr.]] The ''JSR'' also lists athletes frequently misidentified as Jewish, among them second baseman [[Rod Carew]] ("never converted, although his children were raised Jewish"), pitcher [[Mike LaCoss]] ("born Marks, but took his stepfather's name and becomes irate when he is categorized as a Jew"), and quarterback [[Rex Grossman]] (German-Catholic).{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/sports/sports-desk-2007-02-06/48070/ |title=Sports Desk |publisher=The New York Sun |date=February 6, 2007 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} ==Baseball== [[File:KevinYouklis.jpg|left|thumb|[[Kevin Youkilis]]]] In 2009, as Jewish baseball players [[Ryan Braun]], [[Ian Kinsler]], and [[Kevin Youkilis]] were leading in voting for their positions on their [[2009 Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All Star teams]], the ''JSR'' noted that 160 Jews had played in the major leagues.{{cite web|url=http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601079&sid=al9oTr_MYZKk |title=What Does It Mean for the Jews With Youkilis, Braun, Kinsler? |publisher=Bloomberg.com |date=July 2, 2009 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} The ''[[New York Daily News]]'' reported that according to the ''JSR'', there were almost three dozen Jews in baseball before [[Hank Greenberg]], but unlike Greenberg many had changed their names as they played in the majors. Michael Silverman changed his name to Baker, Rosenblum to Bennett, Lifsit to Bostwick, Solomon to Reese, and Makowsky to Markel. And Bohne, Cooney, Ewing, Kane, and Corey were all Cohens in the off-season. When the [[American Jewish Historical Society]] published a set of baseball cards of Jews in the major leagues (in conjunction with Major League Baseball and the Major League Baseball Players Association, and with the support of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum), the project founder Martin Abramowitz of Jewish Major Leaguers Inc. relied on research by the ''JSR''.{{cite web|last=Lowenfish |first=Lee |url=http://www.forward.com/articles/6844/ |title=New Cards Mine Baseball’s Jewish Bench|publisher=Forward |date=March 24, 2006 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}}{{cite |publisher=Boston.com |date=October 13, 2003 |accessdate=May 12, 2010}} Also, when the [[Israel Baseball League]] was active, teams in it would recruit top college baseball players from the ''JSR'''s
